speechtext:
Might I ask the hon.
gentleman how these districts, Markham and Stouffville, voted?

subtopic: MOTION FOR SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO STUDY MORE EQUITABLE READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
In the old riding of York
North I think the party which my hon. friend has the honour to represent in this house won one poll.

speechtext:
And the hon. member
would like those people back?

subtopic: MOTION FOR SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO STUDY MORE EQUITABLE READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
For the information of
the hon. gentleman I may say that I had a very, very substantial majority, and I thank him for his interest.
I can show on this diagram where they took out the village of Stouffville and where Markham was before it was removed from the riding and placed in the riding of York East.
I was also very much interested the other night when we were told of the great care which was exercised in this matter, and when we were assured that this redistribution was not rushed through. Why, they started it at one session and finished it at the next. They slipped in one particular at least; they disfranchised the people in the east half of Richmond Hill. They were not included in any riding, and it was not until after the committee had risen and I drew the matter to the attention of the chief electoral officer that they were added to the riding of York North.
But one might think, after listening to this exposition, that this change was perhaps not based upon population. The hon. member for Davenport was very much interested in the question of population. Just let us see how much there was in that. There were 5,596 taken out of the constituency of York North and a new part containing 5,527 people was added. When the work was completed and
11,000	people were moved, the population was reduced by sixty-nine. I should think there might be some lingering doubt in the minds of some hon. members as to whether perhaps there was not just a little consideration to party expediency when that redistribution took place.
As evidence of the views of the people in the constituency I have telegrams and if hon. members would like to hear them, with their permission I shall be only too glad to read a sample:
In case of redistribution would strongly urge that Markham township be again placed in North York. Being essentially a rural community our interests can only be fairly represented when united in a rural constituency.
That is the point. These people are from a rural constituency, and the wish of the great majority of them is that they should be returned to a rural constituency. On their behalf I am asking only that justice be given to the people of the township of Markham and the village of Stouffville, and that, as suggested by the hon. member for Champlain, the matter be referred to a committee.

subtopic: MOTION FOR SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO STUDY MORE EQUITABLE READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a few observations to offer with regard to the resolution moved by the hon. member for Champlain (Mr. Brunelle). First, I wish to join with the previous speaker in congratulating the hon. member for his motion. While listening, a moment ago, to the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol), I realized that the hon. member for Champlain was perfectly right in raising this question. The resolution asks for the appointment of a com-

Redistribution-Mr. Tremblay
mittee for the single purpose of giving justice to the people of Canada. In support of that statement, I can but quote his motion which is as follows:
That, in the opinion of this house, it is expedient that the Representation Act, 1933, should be amended in such manner as to bring about a more equitable readjustment of the representation in the House of Commons and to effect thereby a more just redistribution of Canada's electoral districts, and that a special committee be appointed to study this matter.
Mr. Speaker, my colleague, the hon. member for Champlain thought fit, a few days ago, to point out as a crying injustice the distorted outline of the county I have the honour to represent in this house. He was perfectly right. The redistribution which must take place after each decennial census was so ordered with a view to balancing the population in the various constituencies and to enable communities about equal as to number to be represented in the house, in so far as possible. When the hon. member showed you the map of the electoral district, he did not mention the size of its population, which I know, of course, better than he does; but if you consult the report of the chief electoral officer for 1930, you will see that instead of balancing the population as between Dorchester and the adjoining counties of Belle-chasse and Beauce,-liberal counties, and known as such-they accentuated the difference in number. Kindly permit me, Mr. Speaker, to quote a few figures. For instance, before the last census, the population of the electoral district of Dorchester was 29,503. The adjoining riding of Beauce had a population of 52,700. My predecessor, who evidently cared no more about the balance which he was to try to reestablish, gave the county of Beauce four parishes that belonged to the county of Dorchester, when the county of Beauce had already twice as big a population as the other one.
Well, you may say that there was perhaps some geographical reason to justify the attitude taken by the former member for Dorchester. In my opinion, there might have been three reasons: the geographical conditions, the psychological causes, and, last but not least, the political motive. As to the geographical conditions, if you will kindly look over this map of the constituency of Dorchester which I am now showing to the house, you will easily recognize a likeness to the sphinx. Look at the features, it is the sphinx. Look at the nose, the chin, everything is perfect. Facing that, there are two other parishes, St. Zacharie and St. Aurelie, which, being a part of Dorchester county for federal purposes since many years, had asked,

only a few years before the general election of 1935, to be reincorporated in the county of Dorchester for provincial purposes. The municipal council, the mayor and the authorities of the parish had asked that these parishes be made a part of the county of Dorchester for both provincial and federal purposes. They readily admitted within the boundaries of Dorchester the good people of St. Aurelie and St. Zacharie, and everybody was happy. Once elected, my predecessor said: No longer will you belong to Dorchester; from now on you will be included in the constituency of Beauce for federal purposes, in spite of the fact that you have just secured, for provincial purposes, the right of being included in Dorchester. Perhaps my predecessor is an archeologist; possibly he is. This morning, as I looked over this map of the county of Dorchester, which I am now showing you,
I felt that he may have been gifted with such a talent. If my predecessor had not taken off the whole area shown here, which, naturally and geographically, belonged to Dorchester, he would not have had this picture of a sphinx. There was just one reason for taking away those parishes; it was neither a geographical nor a psychological reason, because in the county council the authorities of those parishes had requested to be included in the county of Dorchester, which I have the honour of representing here, but there was Mr. Gagnon who thought they were cumbersome, not, as I say, from a geographical or psychological but, to be sure, from a political standpoint, for at the election of 1930, these parishes gave, respectively: St. Aurelie, a Liberal majority of 76, and St. Zacharie, a majority of 173, also Liberal. As a result, Mr. Gagnon requested that these parishes be included in the constituency of Beauce.
From an archaeological standpoint, the sphinx would not have been complete had not something been taken off here in order that its head might be properly delineated. There was a small parish in this first corner, the parish of Saint-Luc. It naturally belonged to the county of Dorchester, that is, to the townships of Ware and Standon; the name of the latter had to be cut in half, because one-half of the township had been included in Bellechasse. Well, my predecessor -I do not wish to insinuate that he had political or electoral motives-cut a hole here in the county, so that the head of the sphinx might be perfect. He made the drawing, he removed the small parish of Saint-Luc and had it included in the county of Bellechasse solely for his own protection. But, some might say, the people of Saint-Luc may pos-

Redistribution-Mr. Tremblay
sibly, from a psychological standpoint, have preferred to be included in Bellechasse. I say no and my colleague from Bellechasse would tell you, if he were here. I like very much the people of Saint-Luc, but the surroundings are somewhat unfamiliar to them in Bellechasse, where they have been transplanted only through the wishes of the former member for Dorchester in this house. That is easily understood; those who, to-day, are citizens of Saint-Luc, formerly belonged to Standon and Sainte-Germaine, which are within the townships of Ware and Standon. Mr. Speaker, these people attended the meeting which my opponent and I jointly held in Standon, and they were there, not as Dorchester citizens or electors-they belonged to Bellechasse at the last election-but they could not understand why, for instance, they, who were legitimate children of the county of Dorchester should have been transplanted into Bellechasse solely through the will of my omnipotent predecessor. Well, Mr. Speaker, f am giving you an explanation for this first hole that was cut into the county of Dorchester. You may say that there was perhaps another reason than the geographical conditions. But I am showing you that it is absolutely unreasonable from a psychological angle, and I have also shown that it was wholly unreasonable from the geographical standpoint. However, I agree that there is a political -reason, and it is this: The small parish of St. Luc, which numbers about 150 voters, gave the Liberal party a majority of 125 votes in 1930, and again a majority of 138 votes in 1935. If you will kindly follow my argument you will see that there is another piece of antique art which I again consider as perfect. You have here the lion's tail, that is the sphinx's tail. You know that the sphinx had the head of a man and the body of a lion. They tried to draw something like a lion's tail. That is how they took away a beautiful parish of which the county of Dorchester was so proud, I mean the parish of St. Maxime de Scott. From an artistic point of view I agree that my predecessor was perfectly right; but geographically and psychologically speaking, I repeat that these people rightly belonged to Dorchester. As to voting purposes, the former member had every good reason to send them to Beauce. Again if you will consult the reports of the chief electoral officer for 1930 and 1935, you will notice that St. Maxime gave a majority of 91 to the Liberal party in 1930, and that after it had been transferred to Beauce county, it still gave the Liberal party a majority of 190, as a protest against what had been done. Mr. Speaker, I wanted to submit these facts
to the house, because I feel that the motion of the hon. member for Champlain is fully justified. I admit that sometimes we may, for political reasons, allow a few small trifling injustices to slip in, but it is unworthy of a man who wishes to represent his fellow citizens in a house like this one to say, for instance, to thousands of people: Although you wish to belong to Dorchester, I am going to ship you to other counties and you will be part of them, simply because at the coming elections I want to be elected, and secure a majority for my party.
Mr. Speaker, if you will permit me, I shall say a few words in English, in reply to my hon. friend from Davenport (Mr. MacNicol), although he has left the chamber.
(Text) Mr. Speaker, a short time ago the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) wanted to know if the hon. member for Champlain (Mr. Brunelle) was asking for a committee to redistribute all the counties of Canada. That certainly is not the intention of the hon. member for Champlain. His motion shows that he asks this house to appoint a committee to render justice. The motion reads:
That, in the opinion of this house, it is expedient that the Representation Act, 1933, should he amended in such manner as to bring about a more equitable readjustment-
I cannot see why any hon. member should be afraid of a motion such as this. I do not think anyone would object if the hon. member for Davenport appeared before the committee which the hon. member for Champlain suggests should be appointed, and demonstrated that such readjustment would be unjust. I think the hon. member for Champlain is perfectly right in asking for a committee to study those matters which were neglected in 1933. I ask the hon. member for Davenport to look at Hansard to-morrow morning and read the translation of the remarks I have just made in French and then tell me whether he does not believe a redistribution to be absolutely necessary in my riding in order to give justice to those whom I represent in this house.
I shall conclude by saying that I do not think any hon. member should object to the motion of the hon. member for Champlain. All he asks is that justice be given to the population of Canada. That is all that anyone who realizes his responsibilities could ask for, and I think the house should unanimously support the hon. member for Champlain.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: MOTION FOR SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO STUDY MORE EQUITABLE READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have from time to time heard that it was the intention of the government of the day, with its large majority, to amend the Representation Act passed by this house in 1933. I do hope the government will reconsider its intention in that regard. I listened with great interest to the speeches that were made by the hon. gentleman who moved the resolution (Mr. Brunelle) and by others who supported it, and I cannot but think they have failed to appreciate just what the difficulties in this country are with respect to a redistribution of seats. The hon. member for York North (Mr. Mulock), for instance, had an erroneous impression as to the powers of this parliament. This parliament, as he pointed out, under section 52 of the British North America Act can increase the representation of the House of Commons. But that has been done. We have settled that at 245 members. There is in the statute a provision as to sixty-five members from Quebec. The Dominion of Canada is now entitled to be represented in this house by 245 members. That is what section 52 provides for. We cannot increase the number from Quebec; we cannot diminish it; we are bound absolutely by the rule that Quebec has a fixed number of sixty-five members, and the ratio that exists between that number of sixty-five members and the population of that province means in the end that Canada is represented by 245 members in this house. Parliament has taken those steps; that cannot be changed.
But what can be changed is the boundaries of the seats. There are those who contend that this should not be done, and I think they are right because it has never been done except to correct clerical errors. Section 51 of the British North America Act provides:
On the completion of the census in the year one thousand eight hundred and seventy-one, and of each subsequent decennial census, the representation of the four provinces shall be readjusted by such authority, in such manner, and from such time, as the parliament of Canada from time to time provides, subject and according to the following rules.
Then follow the rules. Constitutional practice has been uniform that once parliament has completed its duty and made a redistribution, that redistribution is not amended by changing the boundaries of constituencies between that time and the date of the next redistribution. Whether that power exists there may be some doubt, but broadly and generally the rule is that parliament can always amend what it

enacts, can always repeal what it has done. But there are some things parliament cannot do within the constitution, and one of them is to increase its membership beyond 245.
The resolution as it reads certainly contemplates a change being made; it asks that the act passed in 1933 be amended to bring about a more equitable readjustment of the representation in the Housq, of Commons. There can be no change in that; that is settled at 245 members. It is settled as a matter of mathematics that Ontario has eighty-two members. It is settled that Prince Edward Island, for instance, has four, because it is provided by the constitutional amendment that its membership shall never be less than its representation in the Senate. The same applies with equal force to New Brunswick. That part of the resolution is absolutely bad, and I think the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) will admit at once that there cannot be a more equitable redistribution of the representation in the House of Commons. Let us look at the rest of the resolution:
-and to effect thereby a more just redistribution of Canada's electoral districts.
"A more just redistribution of Canada's electoral districts"-that is not very happily put, but it means that the electoral districts shall be altered; that the boundaries shall be changed. Mr. Speaker, I plead with the government not to do that. Not for a minute do I deny that the act of 1933 was not perfect. There has not been a redistribution bill passed by this parliament that has been perfect. My hon. friend the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Cardin) knows of the long struggle that took place during part of three hot days in connection with the redistribution bill of 1933. He knows, as every member of this house who was present then knows, that there was no desire to seek party advantage, as was suggested by the mover of the resolution, because nobody could know what would be to party advantage. That is the obvious answer; nobody had any idea what advantage it might or might not be, because the population had changed. No one could determine what the new electorate might decide.
We were confronted with the situation that in the older provinces there were county boundaries; in the west there were not. In New Brunswick and Nova Scotia there are county boundaries; in Quebec and Ontario there have been county boundaries since the establishment of those provinces, and one of the difficulties which has been experienced particularly with respect to the sixty-five seats

Redistribution-Mr. Bennett
in Quebec is that if you adjust the representation on a population basis you disturb the whole county system. There are a million people or thereabouts on the island of Montreal. If you divide that by 44,000 you will see at once that the island of Montreal would have about twenty-five seats, leaving forty seats for the rest of Quebec. Now I ask my hon. friend who wants to bring about this new change, what is he going to do about that? Is he going to say

and this would be the ideal condition-that one man's vote in Montreal shall have the same weight as one man's vote in some very small county that I might name?

speechtext:
Levis; that is an illustration. Is a man to have the same weight to his vote in every county of the confederation? If so, then at once the island of Montreal must have about twenty-five seats, and the other forty seats in Quebec must be determined by a uniting of counties and a disturbance of conditions which have existed since confederation. Do not let us blink the thing; let us look it fairly in the eye. If the resolution is to be carried into effect it means just that. In Toronto, it is the same story; in Hamilton, the same story; in London, the same story. The city seats will have the major representation in parliament because at the moment there is a larger proportion of the population in urban than in rural centres. If those who are interested in this matter will take the trouble to look at the Hansard of that day, they will find that when a motion was made by myself to refer the redistribution to a committee, I pointed out certain elementary rules which would have to be observed. Although we had settled the basis of representation, although we knew the quota of electors entitled to a seat in this house, we at once frankly realized that if we stuck to that we would do a great injustice to rural populations and bring about such an alteration in the boundaries of counties in the older provinces as would create a disturbance that could not be quieted inside a generation.

subtopic: MOTION FOR SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO STUDY MORE EQUITABLE READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
At six o'clock I had just pointed out that county boundaries had been respected in all redistributions which had been made in this country since confederation.
and by reason of that fact great difficulties have arisen in endeavouring to provide that each vote shall have equal weight in every part of Canada.
I now propose to devote my attention to another phase of this matter. If this redistribution hill is to go to a committee it must involve the consideration of the whole 245 seats, and if the mover desires to have effect given to his contention he must be prepared to see the rural part of Quebec lose a very large part of its present representation. Equally must Ontario be prepared to see the same thing follow.
I am going to give one illustration, because this was a matter that gave me much concern in 1933. In the eastern part of Ontario we have Glengarry, Stormont, Prescott and Russell. If we were to give effect to the principle contended for by the mover of this resolution, one of these counties, if not two, would disappear, and the county of Welland, in which area there is a population of 120,000, would of course be entitled to three members. It now has one. The eastern part of Ontario, by reason of the preservation of county boundaries in Russell, Prescott, Glengarry and Stormont, now returning four members, would lose at least two.
The committee in 1933, considering these matters, were willing to deal with them in what they conceived to be a broad and generous manner, realizing that there was not equal weight attaching to every vote, and they laid down the principle, which I believe the then leader of the opposition (Mr Mackenzie King) regarded as sound, that because rural populations were smaller than urban it was desirable to lower the basis or standard of representation, in numbers, in these constituencies. In Canada there are very few rural constituencies, in fact I think none, that have a population of 44,000. If this resolution means anything it means that the rural population of Canada must be placed on the basis of one man, one vote, equality with the urban population, because the hon. member talks about absolute justice, and absolute justice means just that. It means nothing more and nothing less, involving the adjustment of representation of 245 seats, so that each man's vote shall have equal weight in every part of the country.
I recall the attitude taken by the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier, who came into office in 1896 on a redistribution that had been made by his predecessors in office. Although he went to the country in 1900, my memory is that prior to that date he made no modification in the boundaries of constituencies, because the
3&2

Redistribution-Mr. Bennett
redistribution consequent upon the census could not be made following 1901 because the census had not been taken. Under the census of 191il a redistribution was carried out under the government of Sir Robert Borden. At that time I was a member of the committee and I remember the difficulties we experienced before we could arrive at an agreement. Then there was the census of 1921, with the same difficulty. If we take the basis suggested by the mover of the resolution, I can point tonight to many more inequalities in the redistribution of 1921 than in the redistribution of 1933. What is more, within the sound of my voice in this house there are hon. members who, carrying their minds back, must realize that that is so. Why? Because absolute justice is impossible if you are to give the rural population the position which we have given them and if you are to consider the county boundaries as having any importance and not concede to the cities and their population the same position you accord to the others. The 1911 census was followed by a redistribution by Sir Robert Borden's government, and that was followed by a redistribution on the basis of the 1921 census. A government under the present Prime Minister effectuated that redistribution, and although there were many difficulties and differences of opinion, no one suggested that a new statute should be passed to meet the situation.
Let me recall two or three more facts before I conclude. When the committee was set up in 1932 it endeavoured to reach an agreement. My hon. friend the Postmaster General (Mr. Elliott), if I remember rightly, was a member of that committee. The members of that committee were at once confronted with every one of the difficulties to which I have just alluded, and finally they arrived at what was regarded as a fair working arrangement in British Columbia. As I shall presently point out, that was agreed upon. It is quite right for any member of this house to say that the fact that a committee agrees upon something does not necessarily prove that it is correct and just; but it does indicate that the members of the committee from various sections of the house came to the conclusion, having regard to the difficulties they had to meet, that this was not an unfair arrangement with respect to British Columbia. As regards Alberta, I can readily recall the difficulties which arose in getting in the number of seats in the districts in which the population was in that province. The then member for Bow River, Mr. Garland,

was very much offended at the method that had to be adopted, and the then member for Medicine Hat had to follow up the main line of the Canadian Pacific railway to get his population in.
When I was a member of the committee we had all the seats provided for but one, and it became an omnibus seat, known as Bow River, an area as large as Prince Edward Island if not larger. It was divided by rivers, the great Bow river splitting it in two. In Calgary my position as a member was made more dangerous and difficult by the redistribution. I consented to it gladly in the hope that the committee would be aJble to provide, in the other two seats, adjustments which might be compensatory. The result was that the committee agreed upon it, and there was no discussion in the house, except that the then member for Bow River felt that his seat was rather oddly shaped. And it was; there is no doubt about that. But having regard to the population it was almost impossible to make the adjustment otherwise.
As regards Saskatchewan, when the present member for Melville (Mr. Motherwell), who was then also member for Melville, saw the proposed map he stuck his cane through it; he was so offended. As an old member of this house he contended that it was an indecent sort of thing to change the boundaries of his constituency on the basis of population. There is no doubt, strictly speaking, that if the mover of this resolution is to have effect given to his contention, that seat should not have been left as it was. But at times there is a sense of comradeship among men in this house, and the then member presented his case, thinking it was fair and right that the boundaries of his constituency should not be disturbed. He was not a young man but had served his country for many years and had been a minister of the crown, and so the committee finally agreed to leave the boundaries as he wanted them. Then my hon. friend from the Battlefords had some difficulty about his seat.

In the Manitoba redistribution, of which the hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Leader) has complained so bitterly, the committee had great difficulty, because Portage la Prairie is a city which contains nearly half the population of Manitoba, outside Winnipeg. Should they get their representation vote for vote and thereby have half the -seats, or should there be an adjustment along the lines I have indicated? In the end the general sense of the committee was that it would be unfair to do that. Portage la Prairie happens to be a community of some .size. It was difficult to include in it the surrounding area, but this had to be done in order to be able to provide for the population on any reasonably proportionate basis, and county lines there and generally in western Canada have not become so important. Strange as it may sound, the committee agreed to that redistribution in Manitoba.
We come then to Ontario. I have already sketched some of the difficulties; I am not going to recall them here to-night. But if this motion carries and effect is given to it in the terms in which it is written, it will be very much to the detriment of those who sit to the right of the Speaker. That is all I can say. The hon. member for York North (Mr. Mulock) pointed out certain conditions in connection with Markham. I wonder if he told the house where these places had been in previous distributions. No one knows better than the Postmaster General (Mr. Elliott) about the difficulties in Ontario. The difficulty of trying to balance populations becomes almost like a complicated crossword puzzle in these small communities.
I have already mentioned the position in Quebec, where we find the great island of Montreal and other city communities, such a community, for instance, as Drummond-ville, and a small community like Dorchester. The difficulties can hardly be overstated.
As regards the lower provinces, I was amazed at the statement made the other day by the hon. member for St. John-Albert (Mr. Ryan). New Brunswick had to lose a member on the redistribution. Saint John was a double member constituency, and on the basis of population the loss had to fall there. That is all there was about it. were Northumberland, Kent, each with its quota. Kings and Queens were united as Royal; there was nothing else to do. York and Sunbury had been combined; so had Carleton and Victoria. When the hon. member suggested some ulterior agreement or understanding he surely overlooked the fact that New Brunswick had to lose a member and the only place where this could be done was the double constituency of St. John-Albert.

speechtext:
The minister knows that I am stating the position very moderately when I say that the interest in the matter narrowed itself down to a very few people indeed. We endeavoured to meet the views of the present Prime Minister, and I think we did it fairly well. I recall distinctly I myself took a hand at the map at the time, and the same may be said with respect to others.

I shall content myself with merely stating these facts. There can be no denial of them or of their accuracy.	If we desire
to have an absolutely just redistribution bill where every man's vote has equal weight, it will make a very great change in this country to the detriment of the rural population, and I think that would be unfair. I believe it is sound to depart from a fixed rule of 44.000 for each seat. I could give the populations, but I conceive that to be wholly beside the question. To do at this time what the resolution proposes would be to concede the right of this parliament to pass a new redistribution bill. I am not discussing the legal side of the matter, but I do say that the constitutional practice as crystallized by succeeding governments since confederation is that they have never endeavoured to pass a second redistribution bill. So far as any expression of opinion would constitute a guide it certainly was the view of the leaders of confederation, of Macdonald, who was alleged to have gerrymandered in 1882, I think it was, and of his successor in office, that parliament was more or less functus officio as a constitutional institution when the redistribution had been completed.
See what we are being asked to do. We are asked to say that after every election the successful party can come in and with its majority gerrymander the constituencies, if necessary, regardless of the fact that certainly mot more than one redistribution bill is contemplated by constitutional practice. Parliament always has power to repeal a statute that it has passed. The British parliament is constantly asserting that right, but we are being invited to take a desperate position, one which I think the hon. gentleman who moved this resolution should think over very careful^ and, I would hope, abandon; for he cannot ask us to deal with individual seats; we must deal with them all. Bight here in Ontario what we did to prevent what I call racial animosities in connection with those seats will find no justification except the purpose for which that action was taken. We knew they could not be Conservative seats; there was no question about that, but rather than endanger the situation and engender strife I was advised-and the House of Commons took the view-that it was perhaps desirable to leave those small seats with members in rural communities, and let that great peninsula in western Ontario-I think Welland is the name of it-be represented by at least two members too few. I knew that was not

Redistribution-Mr. Lapointe (Quebec East)
in accordance with the theory that each vote has equal weight, but I could go over all the constituencies, indicate the population of each and point out the anomalies that exist.
I say, Mr. Speaker, that it will be found very difficult to arrive at any conclusion based upon a harmonizing of rural interests and urban claims and the maintenance of some regard for county boundaries, and even approximate any realization of the hope that each vote is to have equal weight in a redistributed country. So, although I know the government have a majority; although I know they have the power; although I know it is alleged that promises have been made, I put this to the Minister of Justice, as the chief law officer of the crown: 1. By constitutional practice has there ever been any interference with redistribution bills except for the purpose of correcting errors? 2. Have we not always had regard to county boundaries? 3. Have we not made a sharp distinction between the number of electors that should be comprised within rural areas as compared with urban areas? 4. Is it desirable, as a matter of public policy, apart from constitutional practice, because a government has come back with a large majority, to have not the minority but that majority complain that the redistribution which sent them to this house was bad? That must be a thought for consideration.
I have no suggestion in the world that this was a perfect redistribution bill. I said in the house three or four years ago that I knew its weaknesses, and I know them now. But I say to members of this house that if they set up a new committee they will find that such a committee, if it is to give effect to the motion now under discussion, will change the whole personnel of parliament; for rural populations then must find themselves grouped together without regard to county boundaries, and urban representation must be increased to a point that certainly will be offensive to the rural electors of this country.
There is just one thing I desire to say to the hon. gentleman who moved this motion. Surely he does not think, when I made the suggestion that we could not have an election until after redistribution, we had any idea as to what the redistribution should be, in dealing with the question of the Ottawa agreements. That was one isolated sentence which he took from my remarks, and I think in fairness he should not have done so. When he suggested that I pointed out that if we could not agree we would have to have recourse to brute majority to wind up the matter because we could not delay it any longer, he overlooked the fact that my one
plea was that we might be able to reach an agreement and obviate the necessity of the majority enforcing its will upon the minority. Those who have read redistribution discussions in other years and who have compared them with the result of. our efforts in 1933, not saying that the bill is good or bad, but with regard to the unity of the committee, I feel certain will have to conclude that the measure of success which attended their efforts was very much greater than or at least as great as that which attended the efforts of committees in previous years. In South Africa they make the redistribution by a commission. In England it is done by judges. In Canada the Liberal party was of the opinion that it might be done by a committee of the house; Sir Wilfrid Laurier was certain that it might be properly done in that way. I think if members of this new House of Commons understood the effort and the time that men devote to an effort to arrive at unity, they would realize just what is involved in a resolution of this kind.
I can only ask the government, with all the conviction of which I am capable, not to open this dangerous question on the basis of the terms of this resolution. If I were to speak politically I can only say that if the motion now before us is carried, nothing would be more beneficial to the party with which I am associated. That is, if equal weight is to be given to every vote in Canada, and justice, in the sense in which the hon. member has used that word so frequently, is to prevail, that would be the net result.

At page 297 of Clement's Canadian Constitution I find:
This section 51 applies only to the readjustment of the representation of the provinces as between themselves, and has no reference to the boundaries of the electoral districts in each province, and it would appear therefore that the readjustment, under this section, is a matter merely of mathematics. May I quote to the house the words of an eminent statesman who was at one time Prime Minister of Canada, and possibly the most distinguished Minister of Justice the dominion has ever had. I refer to Sir John Thompson. Discussing the question of redistribution on June 2, 1892, he made the following statement, as reported at page 3262 of Hansard of that year:
When we come to section 51, on which the hon. gentleman based his argument

He was replying to Mr. Davies, who became Sir Louis Davies, Chief Justice of Canada.

-we come to a section which, I contend, iff not a section framed for the purpose of conferring power upon this parliament to redistribute the seats, but a section compelling parliament to do it after the completion of each decennial census. Section 51 is not an, enabling section, because we had the ability before; it is not a disabling section, because certainly, before we are to conclude that it takes away from us powers which are given to us by section 91, we must find express words that do so. If by section 91 of the act we have all powers given to us in relation to passing laws for the peace, order and good government of Canada, we are not to interpret the act or any part of it as taking away any fraction of that power unless we find words which can receive no other interpretation. But the obvious interpretation of section 51 is that it shall be the plain duty of this parliament at the end of every decennial census to readjust the representation, and then it goes on to say "by such authority, in such manner and for such time as the parliament of Canada from time to time shall provide." If my view of section 51 is correct, that it is not a section under which we derive our general or specific power over this subject, then all ambiguity is removed, and it simply enables us to do that work which is enjoined on us and made compulsory by that section at the close of every decennial census, by some other authority, if we please, as for example, by the provincial legislatures or otherwise. But the hon. gentleman, in order to give effect to the paraphrase which he made of the section, as to settling a principle not permitting a majority to take advantage of a minority, and all that class of expressions which he used, gave, as his own argument implied, a very vague and obscure meaning of the words relating to "such authority, and in such a manner and for such time as parliament shall establish." I repeat very shortly what I have said on the construction of section 51. I contend we had the power before section 51 and outside of it altogether; that we are not to interpret section 51 as taking away from the general power or making any repugnance in the act, and that, above all, the section is not to receive that construction unless that construction is plain and necessary. But if it were intended by the parliament that passed this statute that, although we should have the power to increase the number of members of this house-and that is another point against the hon. gentleman's argument, that there is power given to increase the number of the house from time to time, provided the proportion of representation is not disturbed as laid down by the act-the question of redistribution is something we are prohibited from doing, there is not in the whole act from beginning to end a single negative provision as regards the right of this parliament to do that work. But the construction of the whole act, unless the hon. gentleman is to read into that section which applies solely to the decennial census, unless the hon. gentleman is to read into that section negative words which are not there, comes to this: That while this parliament may redistribute at the term of every parliament, or from year to year even, yet when it comes to the decennial term we have not the power to redistribute the seats at all.

I shall not speak for the other provinces, but I am sure my right hon. friend is not well aware of the situation in Quebec. He was very, very busy at the time of the redistribution, and I would excuse him for not having known every particular change that was made. But I must say that, so far as Quebec is concerned, it was an outrageous piece of legislation that was adopted by the house. My right hon. friend said that we should respect county boundaries. I am more familiar with the Quebec district than I am with other sections of the province. There are between twenty-five and twenty-six seats in this district and the boundaries had never been changed before. When it was necessary to divide a large constituency, two other constituencies were united in order that the change might be made. I might say to my right hon. friend that after 1933 only two constituencies were left with the county boundaries the same as they were before the redistribution. All the others were changed, and I may say in a manner based only upon party expediency. My right hon. friend referred to urban and rural populations and the consideration that must be given in arriving at the unit of representation.
Reference was made to the county of Levis, which is perhaps one of the most glaring instances that might be mentioned. This county had a population of 38,000. As far as I can remember, the unit of representation was
42,000.	Levis should have been left as it was, but what was done? It happened that on the eastern side of the county there were two or three very strong Liberal centres. These were taken from Levis and added to Bellechasse. Bellechasse did not need these additions as it was quite strongly Liberal. On the western boundary other Liberal strongholds were taken from Levis and added to Lotbiniere. This was another case of carrying coals to Newcastle, as they were not needed in that riding. The final result was that the unit of representation in Levis was reduced to 27,000.
But actually the situation is worse than this. Levis is actually an urban constituency. The principal centres in the riding are Levis, Lauzon and Etchemin. The hon. member for Dorchester (Mr. Tremblay) referred to what had happened in connection with his own constituency. My right hon. friend referred to this riding as "small Dorchester." speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a few words to say on the resolution that was moved the other day by the hon. member for Champlain (Mr. Brunelle). In 1867, the member for Levis was Mr. Blanchet, who later became Speaker of the House of Commons. He represented the constituency for more than twenty-five years. He was the grandfather of the minister who represented the Quebec district in 1933, when the redistribution took place. In 1867, at the time of confederation, Hon. Mr. Blanchet, member for Levis, gave that constituency exactly the same boundaries that it had prior to 1931. Nobody had ever suggested or even thought of changing these boundaries. In 1933, his grandson deemed that the constituency where his grandfather had been returned for twenty-five years should have entirely different limits. He decided that several parishes which were liable to vote in such a way as to hurt the Conservative candidate to any extent should be taken away, and they had to draw out new boundaries.
I would not have protested against these changes, I would have understood that a majority had a right to govern and to allot to the various constituencies the limits which could assist their election, but in the case of Levis there has been a crying injustice, against which I deem it my duty to protest. Not only did they draw out limits for the

Redistribution-Mr. Dussault
county, but they put too many of them. In order to show the house what they have done there, allow me to use the electoral map of the constituency. Here is the county of Levis such as it was redistributed. You have here, at the top, in the north, the St. Lawrence river. In the south, the part that was cut off represents parishes which were all situated in the county of Levis, and which were taken away from us. I submit that the constituency of Levis was too much reduced. Everything that you see here is actually in the county of Bellechasse. The boundaries of the county of Levis would be appropriate; Bellechasse would be south and east, Lot-biniere west and the St. Lawrence river north. And is that all? No it is not all, for there remains the lone parish of Breakeyville which is entirely outside the county. As a jig-saw puzzle, I would ask my neighbour, the hon. member from Lotbiniere (Mr. Yerville) to find a place for this parish as represented by this piece of paper, anywhere and how he likes, without using this other piece of paper which represents the county of Lotbiniere. It is a hard task. You just have-I almost missed it-to add here the county of Lotbiniere, just like this, and there, Breakeyville, and you have it. Without using this piece which represents part of the county of Lotbiniere, you cannot find a place for Breakeyville in that jig-saw puzzle that is now the map of the county of Levis.
Then there is the constitutional and legal standpoint, but I wonder whether anybody has a right to introduce into a constituency a parish that is not touching it at all. You could take an island right in front of a constituency, let us say lie aux Grues, for instance, and say: The people of lie aux Grues will vote in Montmagny. But you say to the people of Breakeyville in the county of Bellechasse who live inland, a mile away from the county of Levis. You shall vote in the constituency of Levis. Is that legal? Yes? Very well then. But why don't you say to the people of Maisonneuve: You shall vote in Levis? It is only a matter of distance. When people are absolutely outside a county, one mile away from Levis, and when to get in there they have to go through an adjoining county, namely that of Lotbiniere, or Bellechasse, while being still voting in Levis, I wonder why they are not compelled to go through three or four counties, and be given the right to vote where it will be the most convenient for the party. In this way you can fix anybody's election, and pick the winner. During the war, votes were sought elsewhere; here, they get them 31111-24
in Breakeyville. Whether you get them from the Breakeyville ballot-box or from the soldiers' ballot-box, it amounts to the same thing.
How did this parish of Breakeyville, after being added to Levis, happen to be outside that county? It is because there lies between Levis and Breakeyville the parish of Saint Jean Chrysostome, which formerly belonged to the county of Levis and is now part of Bellechasse. Some might say: It is a Liberal parish, so you need not complain. It is a Liberal parish, that is true, but Saint Jean Chrysostome is still more Liberal, and that is why it was included in Bellechasse. On the electoral map it is still shown as Saint Jean Chrysostome de Levis. Why was it not left in Lews, since it is called "of Levis"?
From the standpoint of geographical conditions, and of roads, from a common sense point of view, consider the position of the Saint-Jean-Chrysostome people. The church of that parish is exactly a mile and a half from the church of Saint-Romuald. Saint-Romuald is the chief town of the county of Levis. The people of Saint-Jean-Chrysostome lived a mile and a half from the chief town of their county. Now that they have been included in the county of Bellechasse, they must go to Saint-Raphael, chief town of their new county. They must travel to Saint-Romuald then to Levis, they must go through Levis and Lauzon, continue to Beaumont, the first Bellechasse .parish along the shore; after that, they travel inland to the chief town of the county of Bellechasse, that is Saint-Raphael seventeen miles farther through the county. People who were living a mile and a half from the chief town of their county are now compelled to travel a distance of twenty-seven miles and a half in order to reach the chief town of their new constituency.
After listening to the address of the right honourable the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) I feel diffident in explaining to the house the case of Levis. There has been everywhere so much suffering, so much dissatisfaction, as he said, that matters like this ought not to be brought up at a time when there is so much grumbling and wrangling; it might be the prelude to more quarrelling. If, in order to avoid quarrels, the blows must always fall on the same people, it seems to me that it is much preferable, to fight in dead earnest and not only to receive blows but to give a few in return.
I would ask that boundaries be laid out for the county of Levis, but they should be such so as to make it possible for the people of Levis to travel throughout the county without going through other counties, so that

Redistribution-Mr. Neill

they may not have to go by way of the county of Bellechasse. Let all the parishes in the constituency be comprised within a continuous boundary.
After listening to what was said by the honourable members who spoke before me,
I deem it my duty to state the wrongs which my constituents are suffering and to request that they be remedied.

speechtext:
Someone behind me says that it was by the members generally. In spite of that I wish to absolve completely of all blame, from my own point of view, and not speaking for anyone else, two members of the house. One is the leader of the opposition and the other is the chairman of the committee, the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Stewart). It was common gossip at the time around the corridors-and such gossip generally has some basis of truth-that the Prime Minister of that day, now leader of the opposition, had repeatedly expressed the desire that there should be a fair agreement and that there should be nothing in the nature of compulsion, and the chairman of the committee was also all that could be desired. Personally he gave me every consideration that fairness could demand. Where the mistake was made was in allowing local groups in the different provinces to dictate the terms. The main committee would have been fair, because the Conservatives in Quebec would have seen that the Liberals in British Columbia got a square deal, and vice versa. But the matter was left to local politicians, and personal prejudices came in, so that a man could get a fine chance to have his enmity, political or personal, vented without appearing to be too keen. That is where the trouble came in.
As regards the district I represent, any action that I could complain of was not in gerrymandering certain classes of voters into or out of the district. The harm that was done, the unfairness of which I complained bitterly, was that they added an enormous area to a district

which it was already impossible to canvass in the course of an ordinary election. Possibly a greater wrong was done, so far undoubtedly as my district was concerned, under the franchise act, which made no provision for what I might call the transient vote, and in connection with that other section in the act which made it possible to hold an election within twenty-one days, which would have meant that eight-tenths of my district could not have been canvassed at all. To give the leader of the opposition Credit, he removed the causes of both these grievances. He allowed the introduction of the absentee vote, which, while it was not carried out in the spirit in which it was initiated, did substantially redress a good deal of the injustice in that regard, and by means of the arbitrary power in fixing the date of the election he gave us more time than was usually allowed under the old act. We had, therefore, reasonable time in which to canvass the district. Consequently in that regard I have no complaint.
The suggestion, however, that the British Columbia members acquiesced in the arrangement in a sense touches my honour and I must contradict it, because I went home and told my people how I complained of the action of the legislature. I cannot afford, therefore, to have it said now that its action was in any way agreeable to me. The vote will show that I was paired against it. But it may be said that I signed an agreement, and I have no doubt the document can be produced to show that I agreed to accept this redistribution. Yes, that is so; I did sign it, and I went further than that, although it was not written in the bond. I agreed not to attack the government on the subject in the house. It will be said that I was cheerful and happy; that I acquiesced in the redistribution. Well, that depends on what is meant by acquiescence. If a footpad shoves a revolver into your spine and tells you to hand over your purse and you hand your purse over to him, it is not competent for him to say afterwards in court, "Your action was a voluntary one; I did not take the purse from you; you handed it over." That is a parallel illustration. Certainly I signed accepting the redistribution. Why? Because I was told in the most positive terms that could be conveyed to me that it was either that or take a great deal worse. Half of British Columbia was to be added to my district unless I took the portion doled out to me, and I thought it was better to take what I got than to be a martyr and have a vast area forced upon me. The British Columbia members are familiar with that phase of the matter. It was through no voluntary action on my part that I agreed to that redistribution.

Redistribution-Mr. McLean (Melfort)
The leader of the opposition predicated a great deal of his objection to the resolution on this. He said that if we adopted it, the one man, one vote idea would necessarily follow. That is to say, an equal value would be given to every man's vote.

speechtext: That is what the resolution says.

speechtext:
I cannot see that the resolution says that. It says "a more equitable readjustment"; it does not say you are going to have the same unit in the cities and in the rural districts. Ever since confederation, almost, there has been a different and smaller unit allowed for the country than for the city. I cannot see that it is at all necessary that they should be the same if this resolution is accepted.
Other reasons given by the leader of the opposition, however, have more weight. It is very questionable perhaps whether it is wise to have a redistribution in the middle of the term. That is a matter of opinion. For my part I shall be guided a good deal by the wishes of my friends from Quebec, who gave me loyal support when I was in trouble in the redistribution, and while I am not particularly keen on the matter myself I am willing to defer my judgment to theirs.

subtopic: MOTION FOR SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO STUDY MORE EQUITABLE READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: Before this motion is dealt with I must say a few words in fairness to the people I represent, among whom this redistribution of three years ago was a burning question for the two years before the election of 1935. The constituency of Melfort is not an old one like many of those in Quebec about which we have heard to-night, but for nearly twenty-five years the base line which formed the south boundary of Prince Albert, out of which Melfort was later carved, was not changed by any government of any stripe of politics. There was a reason why the constituency should be reduced in size, namely, that the population had increased perhaps to a greater degree than in many other districts in Saskatchewan. I know it is difficult to make a redistribution satisfactory to everyone. But when one looks at the map, what was done with that constituency?

subtopic: MOTION FOR SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO STUDY MORE EQUITABLE READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: We cannot see it.

subtopic: MOTION FOR SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO STUDY MORE EQUITABLE READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
Well there are larger maps printed on which hon. members can see it, and it will show to greater advantage-or disadvantage. On the east side a great piece of territory sixty by five hundred and fifty miles was taken off the constituency
31111-24J
of Melfort and added to Mackenzie. Now there was no community of interest between those two pieces of country. Heavy timber separated them. There was hardly any transportation possible by road, and transportation by rail was inconvenient because railway service was given by a new branch line on which there was no regular passenger train. For some unknown reason, however, that eastern and northeastern part of the constituency of Melfort, comprising new farming country, timber land and mining and fishing country, which had always been tributary to the area, was torn from that constituency and added to the almost purely farming constituency of Mackenzie, making it extremely difficult for the member for Mackenzie, no matter how active he might be, to get around among his people. One of the complaints of the people in that area was that almost all their community of interest was bound up with the older part of the Carrot River valley, from which many of them came. I admit that part of the constituency of Melfort might have been taken and added to some other, but there was no reason why that large territory on the east should have been taken.
Then in the southwest part, looking at this map hon. members will find another series of steps and stairways, poll separated from poll just as they happened to reflect political opinion in the election of 1930. The leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) used the argument a little while ago that it ill befitted those who had come back to office in spite of this redistribution to complain of it. I would say that the time to think of that was in 1933 when those who had come into office should have been reasonably satisfied as to a fair division of territory. In the southwestern part of the constituency of Melfort there were, as I say, lines drawn between polling subdivisions according to the way they voted in 1930. It will be found that within a couple of miles of four or five of the principal towns along the one main line of railway in the western part of that constituency, the territory was taken away and added to the constituency to the south. People naturally wanted to go to vote in the towns where they had been doing their business and where their connections were. To those who had been taken out of the territory in which they had been all their lives, reasons were advanced that I am not going to recount for putting them where they were put. But they were amazed and astounded to think that any government would do that to them without fair and adequate reason.

speechtext:
The name was wiped
out, and so were the Tories. But I want to be fair to the right hon. gentleman now leading the opposition (Mr. Bennett). When the matter was brought to his attention in the house and he found out, I think perhaps for the first time that the name "North Battleford" had been destroyed by the committee, he took action. As member for the riding I rose in my place in the house and made representations to the right hon. gentleman to have that disgrace remedied, and he was man enough to rise and move to have the name "North Battleford" retained. That is the only reason why we have that name on the electoral map of Canada to-day.
Wha.t was done in order to gerrymander the riding of North Battleford by this organization within Saskatchewan representing the Conservative party in that province? I happen to live in the city of North Battleford, where I have been in business for twenty-five years. My home is there. The city of North Battleford and about fifty polls running along the North Saskatchewan river were taken out of the riding of North Battleford and thrown into the southern portion of the province. The southern part, that is, the part south of the North Saskatchewan river, is the Battleford area which always belonged to the old town of Battleford and, as far as I can see, should still belong to it. Later, when the west became more thickly populated and development was proceeding northward, North Battleford developed as a great trading and distributing centre, and to-day
it is a city of six thousand people-a business centre for the great northland beyond. Since the time North Battleford started to grow, there has been a riding of North Battleford, separate from the old riding of Battleford. When the report of this redistribution committee was brought into the house, as I have said the name "North Battleford" was destroyed, and they had no name for the riding south of the river. When the matter was brought up in the house they were going to call the southern riding by the old name of Battleford,
Well, Mr. Speaker, I drew the attention of the leader of the opposition to the fact that he could not very well call it Battleford, the old name, because following the change that had been effected the city of North Battleford was in the old Battleford constituency, and consequently it would be necessary to have that name changed to "The Battlefords". That is how the name " The Battlefords" came into existence. It is an entirely new name. The old name was "Battleford." The new name is "The Battlefords" because the two Battlefords are in the one riding, a gerrymandered one.
Just understand what has been done, Mr. Speaker. To-day we have a riding called North Battleford. and we have the city of North Battleford gerrymandered out of that riding. It is not in the riding at all. Surely that is all it is necessary to say in order to let the people of Canada form a clear-cut judgment as to what was done to North Battleford as a riding in 1933. The like of it was never duplicated in the electoral history of this dominion, and I hope it will never happen again. It was absolutely unfair. As far as I am concerned I am not afraid to go back and be reelected for the riding for which I was elected at the last election. I desire to make that clear. I am not making these remarks because there may be any political advantage for me in the change. What I am concerned with is the fact that the city in which I live, North Battleford, is out of the riding of North Battleford which I represent in this house. If you can beat that for a gerrymander I should like to have you do it.
So, Mr. Speaker, I say that this matter ought to be sent to a committee where it could be thoroughly investigated and reported upon as soon as possible. I would say also that certain boundaries-I am not going to say how many, or where-ought to be changed and that a readjustment ought to take place. The sooner that is done the

Redistribution-Mr. Gariepy
better it will be for the honour of this chamber and also for the honour of those who were members of this house when this gerrymander took place four years ago.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a few remarks to make on this resolution, and I wish to make them in French. Hansard will publish an English version for the benefit of those who do not understand our language. The hon. the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe), the hon. member for North Battle-ford (Mr. McIntosh), and the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. McLean) stated that they had cooled down since two or three years and that they had forgotten the injustice that had been done to them. It seems to me that it is not exactly the attitude which this house ought to adopt to-night. If there has been a crying injustice, it should be corrected. Democracy cannot be maintained unless the people be normally and fairly represented.
(Translation) I listened a moment ago to the right hon. the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett), and he showed himself just as I have known him to be for the last thirty-five years, namely a better lawyer than a statesman. He found plausible excuses for the gerrymander and the establishment of rotten boroughs, so much so that I was wondering whether the claims that had been put forward had not been exaggerated. We hear the same kind of complaint from every province. The leader of the opposition, in order to draw in the Quebec votes, or to allay his own feelings or his resentment, mentioned three or four Ontario constituencies which are electing members of French origin or name; but he did not speak about Nipissing, in the same province, which has a population of over 80,000. Take Argenteuil, with a population of 16,000, compared to Drummond-Arthabaska, whose population is 52,000; Nicolet-Yamaska, with 42,000, as compared to Levis, with only 26,000. And the leader of the opposition, affecting the simplicity of a good decent boy, comes here and claims that he was acting in good faith, that he did not know they were preparing a nest in Argenteuil for one of his colleagues, and another one in Levis, and that a certain number of safe seats were created in the province of Quebec, in order to have a handful of tories in Parliament after the elections of 1935.
Insofar as I am concerned, my mind is made up, and, in rising to speak, I am thinking even of Three Rivers where they cut the old traditionally liberal county in two, by taking only the city of Three Rivers, and adding to it seven parishes that, save one, never voted

otherwise than for the most avowed conservatives. They thought that in that nest the man that they since appointed as a member of the Senate could have been reelected as a conservative candidate.
Mr. Speaker, these conditions are not normal, nor fair, and the people are rightly objecting to them. The hon. Minister of Justice asked the mover of this resolution to withdraw it, and he suggested a theoretical study by a committee, according to some sensible method. But I am wondering why this resolution should not be adopted as presented. The motion does not ask for an immediate fair redistribution, but a better redistribution, along with the appointment of a special committee to investigate the question. Then, since others have shown that the gerrymander of 1933 was an abominable thing, why should we not continue making a thorough investigation of the problem, in order to see where a flagrant injustice has been done, even if we have to correct it later or not. This does not preclude consideration of the suggestion made by the hon. the Minister of Justice; it is an excellent one, in my opinion, for I feel that a nonpartisan body would be much preferable for establishing the boundaries. I agree with him on that matter. But I say that it lies outside the scope of the motion as moved by the hon. member for Champlain.
I do not know about the other provinces, but in the province of Quebec we have old constituencies which are communities where bounds of fellowship have developed, where similarity of ideas prevail and where the people are used to working in cooperation. If, from year to year, these centres are cut up, if old parishes are split, one half being added to one side and one half to the other side, if our social community is broken up, the result seems to me inevitable, and I wish to emphasize it before I take my seat. We have in this house five parties; in the past there were only two. After all, gerrymandering was of little importance. A little more votes on one side or on the other side, a liberal or a conservative majority had the upper hand, but a different situation might arise in future, when we see the attorney general of the province of Quebec pointing out in public the existence of a communist party in that province which, for a consideration, is enlisting our young men for service in the Spanish civil war. It seems that a number of passports are now being distributed in a surprising way, to young people who leave our country to fight elsewhere, but who will probably return to sow germs of discord, and give rise

Redistribution-Mr. Walsh
to groups which will foment revolution. I submit that as a means of protecting ourselves against such new ideas, of maintaining our traditions, of insuring the true preservation of our people, we should see to it that our representation, which is the basis of our democracy, is better protected. That is the reason why this resolution should receive a more favourable consideration, in order that a committee may make a thorough examination of the complaints brought to its attention, so that they may not occur again in future.
Mr. 0. B. ELLIOTT (Kindersley): Mr. Speaker, speaking for the constituency of Kindersley I wish to say there are no complaints.
