speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I do not wish to take the time of the house in discussing the matter because, as a new member, I am not very familiar with the ways and means adopted in working out the arrangements at present in effect. I should like to observe, however, that I believe certain injustices were done during the last redistribution. I cannot agree with many of the speeches which have been made in support of the present resolution because I am persuaded that no party as such took part in any gerrymandering. If there was any gerrymandering it was on the part of individual members then sitting in the House of Commons, and not on the part of any particular party as such.

subtopic: MOTION FOR SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO STUDY MORE EQUITABLE READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: It is easily seen the hon. member was not here then.

subtopic: MOTION FOR SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO STUDY MORE EQUITABLE READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
As the minister is aware, I am speaking from an entire lack of experience, and possibly it would be better if in the future, when redistribution is being considered, the matter be handed over to some persons who have not the knowledge of how previous redistributions were effected. As a layman, and one quite unfamiliar with redistribution methods adopted by this chamber, I would go further and suggest that before the next redistribution takes place ways and means be provided to have the matter placed in the hands of an independent body or organization which will not in any way be under the influence of any member of the House of Commons. It is only by such means or by a change in the law as it now exists that we shall get an equitable, fair and just redistribution as is advocated in the resolution we are considering.
I can see where injustice has been done to certain individuals residing within the constituency of Mount Royal, as it is at present outlined. There is a small city on the
boundary line between the constituency of Mount Royal and the constituency of Jacques-Cartier. Previously this city had always been in Jacques^Cartier, but what do we find to-day? One-third of it is now in Mount Royal with the remaining two-thirds in Jacques-Cartier. The line runs down Sixth avenue along the railway track, down Thirteenth avenue, and then zigzags until it reaches nowhere. I could not explain how that line came to be drawn, but it certainly was not drawn with a view to giving the residents in that city fair representation in this house.
A similar condition prevails in the city in which I reside on the island of Montreal. This is a city of 26.000 people. Instead of running the line between the city of Outremont and the city of Montreal, they ran it down a street four streets in from the boundary. This was done in order to put one or two thousand voters into the constituency of Laurier rather than leaving them in Outremont. A new constituency was formed to be known as Outremont, and instead of putting the city of Outremont as such within that constituency, they left part of it in and part of it out.
I cannot agree with the resolution as it is presented, nor can I agree with the remarks that have been made in support of it. However, I do agree that there are certain adjustments which should be made. These adjustments could be made harmoniously by various members of this house, not to their satisfaction but to the satisfaction of their constituents. After all, they are the people who should be considered in a matter of this kind. I feel that there are many little difficulties which could be ironed out to the satisfaction of these people who now have just cause to complain. I understand the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) will make a motion later on. I hope it will not be a means of side-tracking this issue. This matter should be placed before a responsible committee, not a partisan one, which will iron out these minor difficulties.
Many of these 'difficulties did not show up until we had an election. They were accentuated because of the election and we see things now as we possibly could not see them prior to 1935. I assume that the committee to be proposed by the Minister of Justice will be acceptable to the hon. member who has moved this resolution. I trust it will be able to do something in the way of ironing out the difficulties and preventing some of the anomalies which now exist and apparently existed in 1932 and 1933. If this committee can devise some means of appointing an impartial body

Redistribution-Mr. Rinjret
to carry out the redistribution after the next census, then and then only shall we be able to obtain some degree of satisfaction as far as the representation of the people of Canada in this house is concerned.

subtopic: MOTION FOR SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO STUDY MORE EQUITABLE READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had not intended to speak on this motion as I was quite satisfied to let the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) express the opinion of the government on the matter. However, I feel I should say a few words. First, I should like to congratulate the hon. member for Mount Royal (Mr. Walsh) upon the spirit in which he has approached this subject. He has pointed out that one of the peculiarities of the 1933 redistribution is the placing of part of the city of Lachine in the constituency of Mount Royal and leaving the remainder in Jacques-Cartier. I admit that there was no intention to favour the candidate in Mount Royal; it would seem to be more a favouring of the candidate in Jacques-Cartier. There are other discrepancies which could be pointed out.
The leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) has said that we cannot have an absolutely equitable adjustment between rural and urban seats. I share his views when he says that the population in rural seats must be smaller than that in city seats. One complaint about the redistribution of 1933 is that there is a distinct disparity as between different urban seats as well as between different rural seats. In connection with the city of Montreal I am somewhat like the Minister of Justice, I can look back at everything with a smile. But there was a very serious complaint at that time. The population in the urban seats seemed to be based upon their location. Those seats which were Conservative by tradition did not have more than 30,000 population, while the strong Liberal seats in the eastern part of the city contained 45,000, 48,000 and so on. I had the privilege of having the top score of 55,000 electors to whom I had to submit my case.
We see the same discrepancies in the rural constituencies around Montreal. For the sake of the record and not with the idea of raising any partisan issue, I should like to remind the house that the old Laval-Two Mountains constituency was adjusted so that it would take in part of He Jesus. Twc Liberal parishes on lie Jesus were taken away from that constituency and added to a Montreal constituency. Perhaps all this was done to promote navigation on inland waters. This is the seat represented by the former Postmaster General, the Hon. Mr. Sauve.
Somewhat the same thing applies to the constituencies of the former Minister of

Marine, the Hon. Mr. Duranleau. That was the well known constituency of Chambly and Vercheres. This brings out the point mentioned by the Minister of Justice. In the old days when it was necessary to combine two counties, this was done without changing their boundaries. Part of the county of Vercheres was taken away and given as a giftsto my colleague the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Cardin). That was thrown in with Richelieu, which made it a very strong Liberal seat indeed. There was one parish, the parish of Ste. Julie, which had always voted Conservative. That parish was not given to Richelieu; it was kept in Chambly. To that was added, not the county of Rouville, but the Conservative section of the county of Rouville.
I could go right along and point out further examples. Take the county of Laprairie, for instance; it was added to Beauharnois far away. Then they joined both constituencies by a sort of Polish corridor, comprising part of the county of Chateauguay, and that had the advantage of relieving the Conservative member for Chateauguay-Huntingdon of some Liberal parishes.
I admit that the results have not been quite what was expected, and that we should prove good winners and not stress these points too much. It shows that after all redistribution is not perhaps so important a matter as affecting the electoral lists as some hon. members may think. I believe that when a current of opinion is established it does manifest itself, no matter how the limits and boundaries of constituencies are fixed, and I believe with the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) that it is more important to devise new methods and more equitable ways and means of effecting redistributions in the future than it is to go over the mistakes of past redistributions. I am not at all so great a partisan as to pretend that this is the only time there have been complaints about redistribution, for we might as well admit that there have been complaints about most redistributions, and it is much more important to devise better means for making the next one than to dig up the past and see w'hat can be done to adjust existing grievances. Therefore I hope, Mr. Speaker, and am confident that the mover (Mr. Brunelle) will withdraw his motion and allow the Minister of Justice, as he has promised the house to do, to make a motion not to refer back to the 1933 or any other past redistribution but to appoint a committee which will examine ways and means how the redistribution should be made in the future and the advisability of changing our methods in that respect.

Redistribution-Mr. Spence

subtopic: MOTION FOR SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO STUDY MORE EQUITABLE READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I cannot see very much reason why we should get excited in the house and waste hours talking over a trivial matter like the last redistribution. I have seen many redistributions, and to my mind it does not matter very much how you change the boundaries, for if the wave is with the party, they get in, and if it is against them, they get out. I for one have probably suffered just as much by redistribution as anybody else, and yet it could not be helped. It was as fair as any redistribution could be, but one cannot have an absolutely fair redistribution. No one will ever think he has been fairly treated.
The hon. member for Melfort (Mr. McLean) probably has a right to some kick about what happened in his riding, as has also the hon. member for North Battleford (Mr. McIntosh), and yet they are both here in the house. The latter claims that the redistribution committee tried to eliminate North Battleford altogether. I consider these members two of my best friends in the house. They are wonderfully capable; they make able speeches, and love to hear the reecho of their voices, but I do not think anybody takes them too seriously. I think they should follow the advice of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) and forget all about it. Only one election can be held before the next redistribution, so why worry? We are just like a kindergarten here, and if some hon. members could hear themselves outside, they would be ashamed. As I say, if the wave is with a party they get in; if not, they get out. It was that way with us in 1930, and no matter what the redistribution was we would have been trimmed. The wave was with hon. gentlemen opposite in the last election; it was against us, and that is the only reason why they are sitting over there.
The hon. member for York North (Mr. Mulock) was speaking this afternoon, and I am sorry I did not hear all he said. But he knows what happened in that riding to beat our good friend the late Herb. Lennox. Talk about gerrymandering! Why, everything possible was done to get that man out of the riding, and still my hon. friends could not get him out. Now my hon. friend comes in with Mulock's millions behind him, and perhaps we shall never put him out. We may attempt to by hook or by crook because we have to fight an election.
As far as the redistribution committee was concerned, I think they tried to be fair to everyone. No doubt there were complaints. The former Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) thought he was getting very unfair treatment, and probably he was, but matters were fixed up for him and for several other members, and, as can be seen by the vote, although it was small, there was general agreement on that redistribution when it came into the house.
As far as Quebec is concerned, I know very little about it. If anything wrong was done, it should not have been done. I do not approve anything unfair or any gerrymandering or anything ungentlemanly to do someone out of a seat. Let us all be good sports and take our defeat with good grace; let us quit losing time and get down to business.

subtopic: MOTION FOR SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO STUDY MORE EQUITABLE READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
Mf Speaker, I must congratulate the hon. membei for Mount Royal (Mr. Walsh). I think he is very clever. He apparently is in favour ol changing the boundaries of his constituency. He therefore admits that there was at least one injustice done by the Representation Act of 1933. On the other hand his leader is against my resolution, and therefore my hon. friend must be against it. Then he says he would be in favour of the resolution of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe), which is not before this house, and which apparently is going to serve the same purpose as my motion, but he is against my motion, which is before the house.
I was surprised to hear the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Stewart) state the other day that he was chairman of the committee which prepared the last redistribution in 1933. The hon. member for Leeds has the reputation of being a fair-minded man. Personally I look upon him as just and straightforward, and why he tolerated the recommendations of the committee over which he presided in 1933 I cannot understand. I do not wish, however, to change the good opinion I have of him, for I feel certain that at least the members representing the province of Quebec on that committee must have taken advantage of his good nature and kind disposition. Those members have disappeared from the political scene in this house, which proves that " la tricherie revient a son maitre." Be that as it may, the hon. member for Leeds feels himself in duty bound to defend a thing from which in normal circumstances, I am sure, he would be the first to dissociate himself.
I must disagree with the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) when he says that the Representation Act of 1933 was the result of an agreement between the parties.

subtopic: MOTION FOR SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO STUDY MORE EQUITABLE READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
No; the members of the committee.

Redistribution-Mr. Brunelle

subtopic: MOTION FOR SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO STUDY MORE EQUITABLE READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
Oh, the members of the committee, but surely what the members of the committee decided had some reflection in what the parties in the house decided afterwards. The debate on the act covers 360 pages of Hansard and represents a discussion extending over practically ten days, and the then Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) had to invoke the aid of the brute majority to put the measure through. These facts are not of a nature to show that there was agreement between the parties. The contentions of hon. members of the opposition are quite erroneous and contrary to all accepted legal principles. In the first place, some of them at least contended that the act was just, and that in the alternative, if it were not just, there was no available remedy until the next redistribution in 1942 or 1943. I shall not take up the time of the house discussing this point. So many members have already pronounced themselves against it, and the injustices have been shown to be so glaring, that to prolong the discussion would only be a waste of time. To pretend, however, that our laws and institutions do not provide an adequate remedy for all injustices and all torts committed is to state a principle which, I submit, should not be enunciated in this house, for it is not conducive to a feeling of security and peace among our people. There is involved in this issue a principle which should dominate any political viewpoint.
Referring to what I said a little while ago, that some who opposed my resolution had suggested that there could be no remedy until 1943 or until the next census, may I say that when attending law school I noted that our professors always impressed upon us the fact that whenever our common law or statute laws did not provide any remedy for injustices or torts, the law of equity was always available to provide the necessary relief. Clement was quoted by me last week, and also by the hon. member for York North (Mr. Mulock), to show that the government has the right to change the boundaries of constituencies. I submit, therefore, that both by law and in equity the government would be justified in having a committee study the matter with a view to removing the most flagrant injustices committed. I wish to put some emphasis on the purpose of the reso-ultion. It is only to correct errors, to right certain wrongs, and, using the words of the holy book, to make the paths straight.
Let me repeat that practically every representation act since confederation has been

amended; for some reason or other they have been all amended. Even the 1933 act was amended, affecting, if I am not mistaken, the constituencies of Hamilton East and Hamilton West. The Minister of Justice has said he is willing to appoint a committee or to reappoint the committee which sat last year to study this question, and in view of that he has suggested that I should withdraw my resolution.

subtopic: MOTION FOR SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO STUDY MORE EQUITABLE READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
That will serve my purpose, and with the consent of the seconder I agree to the suggestion. Before resuming my seat I wish to tell those who have opposed the resolution-and I am speaking on behalf of these in favour of it, whether they have spoken or not

that we as members are not in favour of imposing ourselves upon the country against the people's wish by way of legislation because that method amounts to force and violence. Let me tell those who oppose the resolution that we do not expect any committee to take steps or make recommendations based only upon ballot boxes but we expect it to take steps or make recommendations based rather upon the convenience and welfare of the electors. Let me tell the opposition that we do not expect the committee which is to be appointed to replace one injustice by another, because we do not believe in the principle of an eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth. All I ask is that fair play and impartiality be shown in a federal law which I deem to be of great importance because of the bearing it has on the vote of the electorate at election time.
Motion withdrawn.
Mr. WILFRID LACROIX (Quebec-Mont-moreney) moved the second reading of Bill No. 10, to amend the Railway Act (Telephone Tolls).
Explain.

The Quebec-Montmorency chamber of commerce have submitted to the board of railway commissioners an application seeking to modify the boundary limits within which the Bell Telephone Company serves the city of

Quebec. In accordance with the view then expressed by the chairman of the board, that they are without any authority as far as the fixing of that boundary limit is concerned, and after agreement with my colleague the Minister of Transport (Mr. Howe), I am presenting this bill to clarify the law so as to allow the board to render judgments in keeping with the facts submitted to them.
(Translation):	IMr. Speaker, some time
ago I was called before the board; of Railway Commissioners, in Quebec City, to represent electors from my county who wished to lay before the board a complaint regarding the Bell Telephone Company's service in Quebec-Montmorency county. In my riding, which encircles the city of Quebec, there are several small industries and industrial centres which have constant business intercourse with the city of Quebec and which need therefore, for the marketing of their products, to keep continually in contact with that city, from an industrial as well as an agricultural viewpoint, and which have to exchange telephone calls with the city every day, even four and five times a day. They must pay long distance toll charges each time they put in a call for the city of Quebec. Even when they are unsuccessful in reaching the proper party, they must perforce pay for their useless call. When the farmers of my riding who market their products in the city of Quebec have to make four or five calls a day, it means a daily outlay of 40 cents. There is moreover a charge of so much per mile which they must pay to the company according to the present rates. If we wish to promote the development of our cities, to allow a more regular intercourse between the rural and urban population, we must provide greater facilities, especially to those people who live in the vicinity of the city of Quebec.
When I appeared before the Railway Board, the Bell Telephone replied: "The expenditures which you demand, which you would have us make would be too heavy for the Bell Telephone Company." So I put the following question to one of the company's representatives: How much would that amount to? The Bell Telephone official could not say. Well now, gentlemen, if we wish to hold back the forces of communism, the best way is to see that public utilities give satisfaction to those that have to foot the bill. Before the Railway Board, I asked the same company, represented by its attorneys: What are your profits? And they answered: We will let you know later. I have here a report of that company showing its profits. How much do they amount to, Mr. Speaker? In 1936-I mean the net profits-they amounted to $8,343,819. And you will note that the total operating costs, for the same year, amounted to $10,748,896. I claim that part of what is called "operating costs" is distributed to the Northern Electric, a Bell Telephone subsidiary company, consisting of a few Bell Telephone shareholders. They are hiding their profits, they dare not distribute them to the Bell Telephone Company, to its shareholders; there is an effort made to hide from the public what the earned dividends really are and the public is even precluded from benefiting by the profits accrued to the company. This constitutes a social injustice. I appeal to the members of this house, and through you, Mr. Speaker, to the people of this country, and I say that, ever since 1927, never has the Bell Telephone made the public aware of its profit, even to the smallest extent, and never has the Bell Telephone given the public the benefit of an appreciable change in its rates.
Once again, Mr. Speaker, are we really anxious to stem the rising tide of communism in this country? The best manner in which to attain that end is to allow the common people, those who wish to live and breathe freely in our beautiful Canada, sufficient means for sustenance, and to provide the Canadian people with public services which are really for their own use.

speechtext:
The house resumed from Monday, January 25, consideration of the motion of Mr. Woods-worth :
That, in the opinion of this house, the foreign policy of Canada should conform to the following principles:
1.	That under existing international relations, in the event of war, Canada should remain strictly neutral regardless of who the billigerents may be.
2.	That at no time should Canadian citizens be permitted to make profits out of supplying war munitions or materials.
3.	That the Canadian government should make every effort to discover and remove the causes of international friction and social injustice.
Mr. 0. B. ELLIOTT (Kindersley): I wish to support this resolution, but I do so with certain reservations. Referring to the first clause, in regard to remaining strictly neutral regardless of who the belligerents may be, I wish to draw a picture of the spectacle that faces us in actuality. There are at the present time, exclusive of the forces in China, 5,000,000 men under arms throughout the world. More than 19,000 military planes are in the air forces of twelve nations; more than 4,000 warships patrol the seas defending trade routes. The world is full of great fortresses, organizations, plants, training equipment, war stores, arsenals and armouries. The world this year will spend $9,000,000,000 on armaments, or over $6,000,000,000 more than in 1913. If war broke out to-morrow, five nations in Europe could launch 17,900 planes into the air: Russia, 4,500; England, 4,000; Italy, 3,600; France, 3,000; Germany, 2,800.
The hon. member for Grey-Bruce (Miss Macphail) remarked that Canada is very fortunate, her defence being three oceans: the Atlantic, the Pacific and the Arctic, with the United States to the south; that more than anything else. I very reluctantly disagree with this line of reasoning, because I have repeatedly seen pictures and read of large transports for the purpose of bringing seaplanes close to the borders of our country, which planes may at any time cause destruction and death to our people. The borders of no man's land are no longer limited to the fighting front, but include the whole civil popula-
[Mr. Howe.)
tion of every country in the world. The recognition of this new danger demands that we take such measures of preparation for defence as are within our power. Beyond that I am not prepared to go until other matters in our national life which I shall mention later have been rectified.
This parliament is responsible for the lives of the people of this dominion. That is a grave responsibility. We must rely on the sincerity of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) when he said:
I want to make it quite clear that we will not necessarily become involved in any war into which other parts of the British Empire may enter, simply because we are a part of the British Empire. It is for this parliament to decide whether or not we will participate in a war in which other parts of the British Empire may be engaged.
I am sure that if, through neglect on my part, the civil population of this country were to suffer death and destruction by not having some measure of protection from invasion, I would be very negligent in my duties, but certainly we cannot keep up with the major nations of the world in armament, and possibly it would be unwise to increase our burden of debt by engaging in any armament scheme of the kind.
With respect to the second clause, dealing with profits made in the manufacture of war munitions and materials, in reply to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) the other evening, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) said:
I share the hon. member's abhorrence of anything in the nature of profiteering. I cannot imagine a more contemptible means of seeking to make one's fortune than by doing so at the expense of the lives of others.
And again:
I think private industry, where it is engaged in the manufacture of munitions and war materials, has to be watched closely, for the very reason mentioned by my hon. friend, namely to see that excessive profits are not made.
I should like to point out to hon. members, however, that profits are not made only on war materials and munitions, as can be proven by a table of war costs which I have in my hand. And we are anxious to learn the results of the investigation into the textile industry.
With regard to the third clause, which concerns the removal of the causes of international friction and social injustice, it is my belief that trading restrictions coupled with the fight for markets by the major nations are the primary causes of war. The four danger points are Germany, Italy, Austria and Japan. These nations will hardly start a war unless it is forced on them by the commercial policies of the trading nations of the world. In other words, should the trading nations of the world continue to require these nations to effect commercial impossibilities, war is inevitable as soon as these nations realize that war is the only alternative to internal collapse. The actions of the present government would indicate that they are

conscious of the possibility of the slaughter of another ten million young lives and the maiming of twenty million more. This inference may be taken from their efforts to consummate trade agreements with all nations, but until recently everything, as far as trade relations are concerned, seems to have been done in order to foment the causes of war while nothing has been done toward preserving peace.
The probabilities of war can be tested by two factors-gold production and ability to pay for imports by shipping exports. The nations I have mentioned do not produce gold in any important quantities, and when required to finance their imports by paying money based upon gold they are helpless, and must fight or starve. The maintenance of a standard of living among the people of a nation requires the bringing into the homes and pantries of that nation the necessities of life, varying in number with climate and locality. Averaged in all the trading nations of the world, however, they resolve themselves into twenty-five classes. Russia is the only nation that has power to produce the entire twenty-five classes within her own borders. The British commonwealth of nations and the United' States of America have power to produce within their own borders from fifteen to eighteen of these classes, depending upon climatic conditions. Then comes a tremendous drop to Germany, Austria, Italy and Japan, which makes them the world's war danger points. Germany and Italy can produce within their borders only five of these classes. Austria and Japan can produce only three. On the basis of an efficient standard of living, therefore, Germany and Italy must import twenty of these classes while Austria and Japan must import twenty-two. Attempts to force them to pay for these imports on the basis of money having a value in gold are useless, because these nations have no gold producing power. The alternative is to keep them tied up commercially until, faced with internal collapse, one of them starts a war, which I believe would develop into a world war. The path of peace is along the commercial highway of fair trading relations, allowing these nations to use exports to pay for imports. This is certainly better than sacrificing ten million more lives. The idea that Canada and the United States can stay out of a world war is absurd.
When trading relations are based upon a barter plan, the cry of cheap labour is usually raised, but I should like to quote one fact which will show how baseless the cheap labour cry actually is. When the British

government recently announced its intention to go into air force defence in a large way, the increase in value of shares in aeroplane companies amounted to more in actual money than labour could possibly get ou^ of the whole program. Zaharoff may be dead, but he must have left a good successor somewhere, if we are to judge from war activities and profits already in process of making.
Many letters are coming to my desk from people in all walks of life requesting that I support restrictions of profits in war materials, careful promotion of defence facilities along our coastal borders, and the promotion of peaceful gestures to all nations. War is not caused chiefly by a lust for territory or prestige. It is also caused by a low standard of living, by a feeling of economic insecurity and by the desire for moral and social emancipation. When war becomes a matter of equal sacrifice for all and special privileges for none, there will be less propaganda in favour of it.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to take part in this debate because I believe I represent a certain type of revolutionary thinkers, and I speak because I consider it my duty to do so. I agree with the mover of the resolution (Mr. Woods-worth) and join with him in his utter detestation of war in any form. No good can come from it to man, woman or child, physically, morally, spiritually or financially; yet I fail to see how Canada can remain neutral. We belong to the British commonwealth and if that commonwealth is engaged in war we are responsible, even though such war might be in northern India, or in Egypt, or in some other part of the empire. Our neutrality would not be recognized by any enemy with a big navy or air fleet.
If we are to remain neutral it seems to me our only alternative is to secede from the empire and start on our own. What could eleven million people do? How could we exist in a land-hungry world? The outstanding example of the impossibility of our position is found in the Ethiopian affair. On the other hand we might join the United States or permit the United States to look after us. Then, if they were engaged in war I wonder where our neutrality would be. What is the difference between allowing somebody else to fight for us, and fighting for ourselves? Therefore it seems to me impossible to remain neutral. An enemy which might capture our country might not give us the privileges we now enjoy. We might not have freedom of worship. It is possible that we

Foreign Policy-Mr. Mclvor
might be captured by an un-Christian nation, and our children would be taught to worship war. I am sure there are a great many Canadians who would say that could happen only over our dead bodies.
I believe the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) spoke wisely when he said that he refused under any circumstances to tie the hands of the nation to a declaration of neutrality. Such a policy would be as likely to invite attack as to stave it off. No doubt Ethiopia was selected by Mussolini as a point of attack because they were not able to hit back with equal force, and were not familiar with modern warfare.
I would not ask the government to do for the country what I would not be prepared to do for myself. If my wife and family were attacked I should like to see the man in this chamber who would get away unscathed after attacking them. If any other man's wife and family in Canada, people just as good as our families, are attacked, it is our duty to see that they are protected. I must admit that I have not risen to that perfection of Christian character where I can say that I will have peace in every possible way. I know it is possible for a man who is hit on one cheek to turn the other also, but I must admit my weakness in not having attained that point of perfection.
I am sure any citizen must give serious thought to the part of the resolution dealing with profits. To have control of all profits we must have complete nationalization of resources-resources from the land, and all other sources. Even the leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation, according to the manifesto of that group, is not willing to go that far. I am willing, however, to agree that profits should be wiped out of this horrible thing, because they represent the price of blood, and I suggest that is a poor basis for wealth. We have noticed some people who made money during the late war, and we know that to-day they are not very happy about it. It should be made known that services will be given at wages equal to those gained by the men in the trenches. As wealth is of less importance than human life, wealth should be conscripted first.
We all believe in war. Hon. members may think that is a peculiar statement, but as I sit in the chamber and listen to hon. members who take part in the debates I feel the sword thrusts of political warfare and I hear speakers who are anxious to give the thrust that will
fatally wound their opponents, so that they will be sent back to be buried forever in their constituencies.
If we are not prepared to be absolutely unselfish I do not see how we can say we do not believe in war. We must work for peace, and to me there is only one cure, namely, following the Prince of Peace. During the present session I have been agreeably surprised to find Christian courtesy between the Prime Minister and the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett). I think both these men must have in their private lives places where they can go to be quiet and get built up.
What is the cure for war? It can be cured only by following absolutely the Prince of Peace. As that old philosopher Socrates once said to a group of youths who were bothering him a little by asking how they could get to Mount Olympus, "Keep going in that direction." Anything that will cure hate in an individual will cure it in a nation. I am convinced that there are groups of people all over Canada to-day who are leading a Christian revolution which will help to cure the curse of war.
